Perfect gauge readout reduces the two Pauli channels to classical repetition inference in perpendicular directions. A bare logical X may be placed on any complete row and a bare logical Z on any complete column; parallel representatives differ only by gauge action. views.description: Expanding every polynomial monomial as a torus translation produces two sparse binary CSS matrices. Stacking their X and Z rows in symplectic form is the universal executable baseline used for rank, logical, and distance computations.

A and B are sparse elements of F_2[x,y]/(x^l-1,y^m-1). Monomials are torus translations, transpose reverses a translation, and the two CSS check families are assembled without solving pairwise commutation constraints.

The polynomial ring is the regular representation of the abelian group Z_l x Z_m. This view isolates the exact reason A and B commute and places BB codes inside two-block group-algebra codes without identifying the two families.

The matrices form the three-term CSS complex R -> R^2 -> R with boundary maps [B;A] and [A|B]. Logical operators are middle homology classes, and the gross code's twelve logical qubits are the quotient dimension left after the two rank-66 boundary maps.

Each weight-six check joins three qubits in each data layer. The Tanner incidence can be split into two planar degree-three coupling layers, turning sparse monomials into a concrete syndrome-extraction graph while keeping the schedule and detector model separate from the static code.

The common quotient R/(A,B) controls the number of encoded qubits. Polynomial factors and common roots explain when that quotient appears, why finite blocks can have high rate, and why the studied subclass is not an asymptotically good family.

The same polynomial ideal can be read as excitation sectors, mobility constraints, and logical strings through a Koszul complex. This view exposes topological frustration and blocks the shortcut of declaring every finite BB code a trivial stack of independent toric codes.

For decoding, selected symmetries reduce parts of the syndrome problem to toric-code-like cylinders on which matching applies. The reduction is an operational decoder dictionary, not a global phase equivalence.

views.description: For H1 of shape m1×n1 and H2 of shape m2×n2, the executable convention is HX = [H1⊗I_n2 | I_m1⊗H2^T] and HZ = [I_n1⊗H2 | H1^T⊗I_m2]. Expanding these two binary blocks gives the ordered sparse-Pauli baseline used by the verifier; no geometric layout or decoder is implied by the matrix formula.

Read each Hi as a map from an ni-dimensional bit space to an mi-dimensional check space. Qubits occupy bit1⊗bit2 and check1⊗check2. X checks occupy check1⊗bit2, while Z checks occupy bit1⊗check2. This four-space typing fixes every transpose and tensor identity before a matrix is multiplied.

The same four spaces form the middle portion of a product chain complex. Applying either factor map in the two possible tensor directions creates the two check blocks. The boundary-of-a-boundary cancellation is exactly the CSS commutator cancellation, so the homological and Kronecker-block descriptions are two readings of one ordered construction.

If ri is the binary rank of Hi, the two qubit sectors contain n1 n2 and m1 m2 coordinates. The logical dimension splits into a kernel–kernel contribution (n1-r1)(n2-r2) and a transpose-kernel contribution (m1-r1)(m2-r2). The general constructor helper recomputes both terms and rejects disagreement with the stabilizer rank.

Factor kernels and transpose kernels supply canonical row- and column-shaped representatives, while quotienting by factor images identifies representatives of the same quantum logical class. These shapes are useful to ReShape and related algorithms; they are not extra logical qubits and do not make an arbitrary correction maximum likelihood.

ReShape uses HGP logical shapes under its stated factor and error conditions; erasure decoders are given the lost support; Viderman-style and iterative decoders require declared expansion or update hypotheses; BP-OSD is a generic sparse-matrix benchmark. These inputs and guarantees are not interchangeable, and none yields one decoder for every binary factor pair and every syndrome model.

A factor symmetry or symplectic matrix first specifies a logical Clifford action. A physical protocol must then realize it by transversal layers, partitions, defects, measurements, or other declared resources, and a fault-tolerance argument must control faults through that protocol. Targeted-Clifford constructions and product-code no-go results constrain different layers, so neither is a construction-wide gate label.

Restricting or coupling the factor matrices creates HGP output subclasses; reducing redundant sectors changes the formula under extra algebraic hypotheses; changing to a multi-factor non-CSS product changes the construction itself; embedding one fixed output in a planar device changes only its realization. Output entries therefore point inward with typed product_of relations rather than being treated as aliases of HGP.

Sparse algebraic checks may still connect distant hardware qubits. A realization must add an interaction graph, ancillas, a measurement schedule, fault propagation, and a decoder for repeated records. Distance-preserving circuits and non-local-resource studies solve declared architecture problems; they are not outputs of the bare tensor formula.

views.description: Applying the symmetric hypergraph product expands the finite factor into sparse binary X- and Z-check matrices. Their stacked symplectic rows are the executable baseline for commutation, rank, logical witnesses, and finite-distance checks.

Write the classical parity matrix H as a biregular bipartite graph with variable side A and check side B. For every nonempty S within the chosen cutoff, compare its distinct neighborhood with Delta times |S|. The decoder theorem needs this inequality independently on A and B with both deficit parameters strictly below one sixth; a spectral-gap label or expansion of the later quantum Tanner graph is not a substitute.

Apply HGP(H,H). Physical qubits split into A-by-A and B-by-B sectors, while X checks occupy B-by-A and Z checks occupy A-by-B. Each CSS row combines one factor incidence with its transpose partner. The two mixed Kronecker terms therefore appear twice in HX HZ^T and cancel over GF(2).

Given a perfect stabilizer syndrome, inspect subsets contained inside one bounded stabilizer support and apply a subset whose flip decreases syndrome weight enough. Expansion ensures that a sufficiently small adversarial error exposes a useful move and that zero syndrome below the protected scale cannot conceal a logical class. This is a generator- local greedy decoder, not bitwise majority voting.

The founding small-set-flip theorem treats bounded-weight adversarial Pauli errors with perfect syndrome. The later random-error analysis uses probability to exclude bad local structures, and peeling follows resolvable erasure structure. These are three statements with different inputs and failure events; none licenses one model-free threshold.

A kernel word of H can be lifted into one HGP product sector to give a quantum logical witness. The HGP distance theorem combines the classical distance of H with the transpose distance of H^T. The finite constructor exhausts both small kernels and exports one lifted logical, but scalable lower-bound certification remains a separate problem.

Bounded check weight does not imply bounded-depth nearest-neighbor extraction in a low-dimensional layout. Expansion distributes Tanner neighbors non-geometrically, so a device needs long-range couplers, routing, or growing local depth. Theoretical constant-overhead recovery accounts for a full architecture; it is not an experimental realization of the finite blocks exported here.

views.description: Duplicating the four binary Hamming rows into X and Z sectors gives eight commuting symplectic generators. This executable matrix fixes qubit and syndrome ordering for rank, centralizer, and exact-distance calculations.

Order the columns as 0001, 0010, ..., 1111. Every nonzero four-bit syndrome is therefore the address of exactly one physical qubit. The four coordinate rows are mutually orthogonal over F_2, so duplicating them as X and Z checks produces a commuting CSS presentation.

A single X error anticommutes with the Z checks in the column named by its location, and a single Z error gives the same address in the X syndrome. A Y error activates both sectors. Thus the classical Hamming lookup rule survives intact, once for each Pauli component.

The [[15,7,3]] stabilizer is a strict subgroup of the repository's [[15,1,3]] quantum Reed–Muller stabilizer in the shared nonzero-vector qubit order. Their four X checks agree. The Hamming Z row space sits inside the Reed–Muller Z row space, whose six additional independent rows fix six Hamming logical Z values and leave one protected qubit.

GL(4,2) acts on the fifteen nonzero column labels. Each invertible linear relabeling preserves the Hamming row space, hence gives a physical coordinate permutation that preserves the stabilizer. Its logical action must still be reduced in the fourteen-dimensional logical symplectic quotient; it is not merely a relabeling of seven named logical qubits.

The word “Hamming” refers to the inherited classical parity-check construction, not saturation of the nondegenerate quantum Hamming bound. The constructor-derived n, k, and distance leave unused syndrome space after all single-qubit Pauli errors are counted.

Regard the one-to-fifteen encoding isometry as a tensor with one logical leg and fifteen physical legs.
